source: Partner Analysis Playbook (Leila), worked examples FY2025 Almarai vs SADAFCO

layers.name: Business model
layers.governing_question: How does this company make money, and what protects it?

layers.name: Operating
layers.governing_question: How well does it make and sell, and where does profit come from?

layers.name: Investment
layers.governing_question: How much capital does it need, and what does that capital earn?

layers.name: Financing
layers.governing_question: Who paid for the capital, at what cost and with what risk?

value_equation.value_created: (ROC - WACC (Financing)) x invested capital; growth multiplies the spread, positive or negative
value_equation.golden_rule: investment decisions create value; financing decisions mostly move ROE and risk - never mix them

method: Translate: turn the question into a ratio - name the numerator and the denominator.
Classify: name the lens (business model, operating, investment or financing). Pick the denominator that matches.
Predict: write your prediction from the business model BEFORE opening the numbers.
Calculate: get the numbers for each company separately. To explain a gap, switch to a form that adds up.
Explain & size: link each part of the gap to a real asset or activity, say how much it explains, and whether it is permanent or temporary.
Conclude: say what it means for ROC, growth, risk and value. End with a decision.
pyramid: Answer: one sentence, with a number.
Reasons: two or three causes, each sized.
Evidence: the ratios and notes that prove each reason.
So what: permanent or temporary? Effect on ROC, growth, risk and value.
Decision: what the client should do.

error_patterns.Wrong lens: Explaining turnover with debt, or operating leverage with CWIP.
error_patterns.No so what: A number without its consequence for value.
error_patterns.Unsized reason: Because of X without how much of the gap X explains.
error_patterns.Circular answer: Explaining a ratio with itself, or with its own result.

questions.question: Where does the company start and end in the value chain? What does it buy, make, own and outsource?
questions.why: The starting point decides capital intensity, cost structure and risk. Every later answer depends on it.
questions.where_to_look: Business description (annual report); cost-of-sales note (materials vs other costs); fixed-asset note (land, herds, plants, fleet); segment note.
hypotheses: H1 Integrated upstream: owns raw-material sources → low materials ratio, heavy assets.
H2 Converter / brand owner: buys processed inputs → high materials ratio, light assets.
H3 Outsourced maker or distributor: very high materials ratio, very low PPE.
careful: "Both are food companies" is not an answer.
Leased assets hide what is really used: check right-of-use assets.
A low materials ratio is not efficiency: the cost may have moved to depreciation and staff.
questions.related: Depreciation ÷ revenue; staff costs ÷ revenue; gross margin; capital turnover.
questions.answer_structure: "[Company] starts at [stage] and ends at [stage]. It owns [assets] and buys [inputs]. Evidence: materials x% of revenue, assets y× revenue vs peer z×. Consequence: [capital intensity, cost type, main risk]."
questions.worked_example:
Almarai owns feed, herds, poultry farms, plants and fleet: materials 42%, total assets 1.8× revenue.
SADAFCO buys milk powder, manufactures and distributes: materials 55%, total assets 0.9× revenue.

questions.question: What does it sell, and which segment drives revenue, profit and capital?
questions.why: The biggest revenue segment is often not the biggest profit segment. Mix moves the group margin.
questions.where_to_look: Segment note: revenue, profit and assets by segment.
key_ratio: Segment share of revenue, profit and assets
hypotheses: H1 One dominant segment drives everything.
H2 Revenue leader ≠ profit leader: a hidden gem or a capital sink.
H3 Mix is shifting toward the lower-margin segment.
careful: Segment profit definitions differ (before or after allocated costs).
A change in allocation method breaks the trend.
A revenue share alone says nothing.
questions.related: Mix effect vs rate effect on the group margin; segment asset growth.
questions.answer_structure: "[Segment] = x% of revenue, y% of profit, z% of assets. Mix is moving from [A] to [B], worth ±n pts of group margin. The segment to watch is [C] because [reason]."
questions.worked_example:
Almarai Bakery: 13% revenue, 18% profit, 5% assets (hidden gem). Poultry: 18% revenue, 28% assets, 4.4% return (capital sink).
SADAFCO Drinks 54% of revenue (61% in FY20), margin 15.8% vs 8.1% for non-drinks.

questions.question: Who buys, through which channel, and who holds the bargaining power?
questions.why: Powerful buyers take margin through rebates and promotions, even when prices look stable.
questions.where_to_look: Revenue note (gross-to-net, rebates); receivables note (concentration); expense notes (trade promotion, A&P); MD&A.
hypotheses: H1 Modern retail is powerful → rebates rising.
H2 Fragmented traditional trade → own fleet, higher distribution cost.
H3 Institutional contracts → stable volumes, thin margins.
careful: Revenue is usually reported net of rebates: the gross-to-net trend is hidden unless disclosed.
Stable DSO can hide rising rebates.
questions.related: Selling & distribution ÷ revenue; A&P ÷ revenue; DSO trend.
questions.answer_structure: "Main channel: [channel]. Bargaining power sits with [party]: rebates rose from x% to y% of revenue. Effect: −n pts of margin, and [implication]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai rebates 1.9% → 2.9% of revenue. SADAFCO trade promotions 1.7% → 3.5%. Retailers are taking more from both.

questions.question: Where does it earn, and what risks come with each country?
questions.why: Each country brings its own growth, inflation, currency and cost of capital.
questions.where_to_look: Geographic note; FX and risk notes; country inflation data.
key_ratio: Revenue share and growth by country
hypotheses: H1 Home-market concentration: single-country risk.
H2 Diversification that adds currency risk.
H3 Growth coming from a non-core market.
careful: Nominal growth in high-inflation countries is not volume.
FX translation can create or hide growth.
questions.related: Country risk premium and revenue-weighted ERP; FX losses; margin by country.
questions.answer_structure: "x% of revenue comes from [country]. Growth was driven by [country] (+SAR n m). Main risk: [FX / country]. Effect on cost of capital: [ERP choice]."
questions.worked_example:
Almarai: 66% Saudi, 13% Egypt and Jordan (Egypt devalued 39% in 2024).
SADAFCO: 77% Saudi; Poland (+SAR 106m) brought all of FY25 growth.

questions.question: How is revenue earned: repeat daily purchases, contracts or one-off sales? Is it seasonal?
questions.why: Repeat, everyday demand makes revenue stable and lowers risk. Seasonality moves working capital.
questions.where_to_look: Business description; quarterly reports; revenue recognition note.
key_ratio: Share of revenue from repeat or contracted sales
hypotheses: H1 Daily repeat consumption: defensive revenue.
H2 Seasonal peaks (summer, Ramadan) drive stock and cash swings.
H3 Contract or tender based: lumpy revenue.
careful: Annual numbers hide seasonality: year-end working capital may not be typical.
questions.related: Inventory days at year-end vs average; quarterly margins.
questions.answer_structure: "Revenue is [repeat / seasonal / contract]: [evidence]. Consequence for risk and working capital: [effect]."
questions.worked_example: Both sell daily perishables and staples: defensive demand. Ice cream (SADAFCO) peaks in summer.

questions.question: What are the industry's economics: growth, margins and returns? Where is the profit pool?
questions.why: A company's numbers mean nothing without the industry benchmark.
questions.where_to_look: Industry data (Damodaran by sector); peer annual reports.
hypotheses: H1 Above the industry: an advantage to explain.
H2 In line: a commodity player.
H3 Below: structural disadvantage or an investment phase.
careful: Wrong peer set (global vs local, different business models).
One year vs the industry average is not enough.
questions.related: Peer ROC, peer margins, peer turnover.
questions.answer_structure: "The industry earns x% on capital; [company] earns y%. The gap of n pts comes from [margin / turnover], because [business reason]."
questions.worked_example: Global food processing after-tax ROC ≈ 12% (Damodaran, Jan-2026). Almarai 9.1% (below); SADAFCO 33.9% (far above).

questions.question: What is its market share, and is it rising or falling?
questions.why: Share trends show whether growth comes from winning customers or from the market.
questions.where_to_look: Annual report (Nielsen data); MD&A; real growth vs category growth.
hypotheses: H1 Leader gaining share.
H2 Leader losing share to challengers or imports.
H3 The whole category is shrinking.
careful: Share bases change between reports.
Value share rises with price increases even when volume share falls.
questions.related: Real growth; A&P spend; trade promotions.
questions.answer_structure: "#n in [category] with x% share (from y%). Growth vs category: ±n pts. Reading: [share gain / loss / category change]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO is #1 in UHT milk, tomato paste and ice cream, yet Saudi real volume fell ~1.6% in FY25: share loss or category decline? Ask management.

questions.question: What protects its returns, and can you prove it with numbers?
questions.why: Only a lasting advantage keeps ROC above WACC. It is the biggest driver of terminal value.
questions.where_to_look: ROC and WACC history (5–10 years); margin stability; peers.
hypotheses: H1 Brand: shows as pricing power and high gross margin.
H2 Scale or network: shows as lower costs or a hard-to-copy distribution system.
H3 No moat: returns follow the cycle.
careful: One good year is not a moat: show persistence and name the source.
A high ROC can come from old, fully depreciated assets.
questions.related: Pass-through; market share; gross margin stability; erosion signals (rebates, A&P cuts).
questions.answer_structure: "Spread +x pts, positive in n of m years. Source: [named source], shown by [evidence]. Erosion signals: [list]. Verdict: wide / narrow / no moat."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO: average spread +27 pts, brand + freezer network. Almarai: +1.2 pts, cold-chain scale. Both: narrow moat.

questions.question: Can it pass input-cost increases to customers, and how fast?
questions.why: Pricing power decides how much margin survives a commodity shock.
questions.where_to_look: Materials ÷ revenue over a commodity cycle; commodity indices; hedging note.
key_ratio: Pass-through = own price increase ÷ cost inflation
hypotheses: H1 Full and fast pass-through.
H2 Partial and lagged.
H3 'Rockets and feathers': prices kept high when costs fall.
careful: Inventory and hedges delay cost effects: one year misleads.
A price rise can cost volume.
questions.related: Gross margin trough to peak; inventory days; volume trend in the same years.
questions.answer_structure: "In [shock year] costs rose c% and prices p%: pass-through n%. Margin recovered by [year]. Lag comes from x days of inventory."
questions.worked_example: Almarai passed on ~50% in 2022; cumulative ~42% by 2025.

questions.question: Which inputs drive costs, and who sets their price?
questions.why: If the main input is a world commodity, margins follow a market the company does not control.
questions.where_to_look: Cost-of-sales note; commodity-risk note; hedging note.
key_ratio: Hedged share of the input bill
hypotheses: H1 World commodity (powder, grains).
H2 Local regulated price or subsidy.
H3 Own production: the cost is internal.
careful: Subsidies can end.
Hedges often cover a small share.
questions.answer_structure: "x% of revenue goes on [input], priced by [market]. Hedges cover y%. A 10% rise costs n pts of margin."
questions.worked_example: Almarai hedges only ~3–9% of materials. SADAFCO's materials rose 4.6 pts of revenue in FY25.

questions.question: How much capacity does it have, and how full is it?
questions.why: Spare capacity means profit can grow without capex. Full capacity means capex is coming.
questions.where_to_look: Capacity data in the annual report; CWIP; capex plan.
hypotheses: H1 Running full → capex needed.
H2 Spare capacity → operating-leverage upside.
H3 Building ahead of demand → turnover falls first.
careful: Capacity in tonnes vs revenue in riyals.
New plants take years to ramp up.
questions.answer_structure: "Capacity [x], utilisation ~y%. New capacity of [z] due [year]. Effect: [turnover / margin]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO dairy capacity 540,000 tonnes. Almarai: SAR 18bn plan, SAR 5.8bn of CWIP.

questions.question: Which activities should it own rather than buy, and does integration pay?
questions.why: Owning more stages adds capital. It creates value only if it adds margin, security or share.
questions.where_to_look: Segment note; peers with different models; capital per SAR 100 of sales.
key_ratio: Capital per SAR 100 of sales vs peer
hypotheses: H1 Integration buys quality and supply security worth the capital.
H2 Integration only moves profit from the P&L to the balance sheet.
H3 Integration destroys value: returns below WACC.
careful: Same margin with more capital means lower ROC.
The strategic benefit must appear in price, share or stability.
questions.related: Margin, turnover and ROC vs peer.
questions.answer_structure: "Integration ties up x of capital per SAR 100 of sales vs y for the peer, for the same margin. It pays only if [benefit], shown by [evidence]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai needs 150 of capital per SAR 100 of sales vs 39 for SADAFCO, for the same ~12.7% after-tax margin.

questions.question: What does government policy give or take?
questions.why: Grants and protection can inflate margins. Their removal is a hidden risk.
questions.where_to_look: Government grants note; zakat note; regulatory disclosures.
hypotheses: H1 Subsidies inflate the margin.
H2 Regulation protects (import rules, licences).
H3 Policy risk: price caps or subsidy removal.
careful: Grants are often netted inside cost of sales.
Zakat is not income tax: the tax shield on debt is small.
questions.answer_structure: "Policy contributes x% of EBIT. It is at risk if [change]. Margin without it: y%."
questions.worked_example: Almarai's materials are shown gross of grants; fading subsidies are a moat-erosion signal.

questions.question: What has management done with past capital and cash?
questions.why: Past allocation is the best guide to how new capital will be used.
questions.where_to_look: Five-year cash flow statement; acquisitions note; dividend history.
hypotheses: H1 Disciplined reinvestor.
H2 Over-distributor: pays out more than it earns.
H3 Empire builder: invests at low returns.
careful: Judge by returns, not by size.
One acquisition can define a decade.
questions.related: Reinvestment rate; payout ÷ free cash flow.
questions.answer_structure: "Over five years management spent SAR x on [projects], y on dividends. New capital earned z%. Verdict: [type]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO paid out 114% of profit in FY25. Almarai reinvested 144% of NOPAT in 2025; poultry earned 7.6% on new capital.

questions.question: What three things could break the business model?
questions.why: A partner ranks risks by impact and probability, and puts a number on each.
key_ratio: Impact in SAR m or pts of margin for each risk
hypotheses: H1 Commodity input shock.
H2 Customer or channel power.
H3 Country, FX or regulatory change.
careful: A list of risks is not an analysis: rank and quantify.
questions.related: Sensitivities from the operating and financing sheets.
questions.answer_structure: "Top three risks: (1) [risk]: trigger, impact −n, mitigation. (2) … (3) …"
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO: powder prices, Saudi volume decline, payout above free cash. Almarai: feed shock, plant ramp-up, debt during the capex peak.

questions.question: Can you explain how it makes money in one sentence, with its key number?
questions.why: If you cannot say it in one sentence, you do not understand it yet.
hypotheses: H1 Margin-led model.
H2 Turnover-led model.
H3 Both.
careful: Do not list activities: state the mechanism and the number.
questions.answer_structure: "[Company] makes money by [mechanism], using [assets], and earns x% on capital because [reason]."
questions.worked_example: "SADAFCO turns imported powder into Saudia-branded milk and ice cream, and earns 34% on capital because it owns brands and distribution, not farms."

questions.question: How fast is revenue growing, compounded, and how does that compare with its history?
questions.why: Growth is the first value driver, but only after you know where it comes from.
hypotheses: H1 Steady growth.
H2 One spike year inflates the average.
H3 Slowing growth.
careful: Check that windows match (year-end changes, 9-month periods).
Use CAGR, not the simple average.
Use restated figures (discontinued operations).
questions.related: Volume vs price (OP-02); growth by segment (OP-03).
questions.answer_structure: "Revenue compounded x% a year over [period] (latest y%). Read: [steady / spike / slowing], because [driver]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 7.5% (2020–25); SADAFCO 6.8% (Mar-20 to Dec-25). Both inflated by one inflation year.

questions.question: How much of growth is price, volume, mix, acquisitions and FX?
questions.why: Only volume growth lasts when prices fall.
questions.where_to_look: Segment note; MD&A; inflation data; acquisitions note.
key_ratio: Own price ≈ (1 + cost inflation) × last year's materials ratio ÷ this year's − 1
hypotheses: H1 Volume-led: lasting.
H2 Price-led: fades with commodities.
H3 Acquisition-led: bought, not organic.
careful: "COGS grew less than revenue, so it was price" fails when input costs move.
Acquisitions inflate organic growth.
questions.answer_structure: "Growth g% = price p% × volume/mix v% (+ acquisitions a%). The lasting part is [v%]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 2022: +18% = 7.6% price × 9.8% volume, mix and acquisitions. SADAFCO FY23 +22%: mostly price.

questions.question: Which segments and countries contributed to growth, in points?
questions.why: Group growth can hide a shrinking core.
key_ratio: Contribution = segment growth × last year's share
Change in SAR m by segment
hypotheses: H1 Broad-based growth.
H2 One segment or country carries the group.
H3 Core is shrinking under the average.
careful: Small bases grow fast: look at SAR m, not only %.
questions.answer_structure: "Of g% growth, [segment] gave x pts, [segment] y pts. The core [grew / shrank] by z%."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO FY25: Poland +SAR 106m, Saudi −11m, other GCC −58m.

questions.question: What is the gross margin: level, trend, and the year it broke?
questions.why: Gross margin shows the value added on the product before overheads.
key_ratio: Gross margin = (revenue − cost of sales) ÷ revenue
hypotheses: H1 Input costs moved.
H2 Prices changed (pass-through or promotions).
H3 Mix changed.
careful: Gross margins are not comparable when one company records depreciation or farm costs in cost of sales and another does not.
questions.answer_structure: "Gross margin x% (peer y%), trend [direction] over five years. Break in [year]: −n pts, caused by [line]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 31.2%; SADAFCO 31.1%. SADAFCO fell 4.6 pts in FY25 (35.7% → 31.1%) on materials.

questions.question: Which costs are variable and which are fixed?
questions.why: The split decides operating leverage and how profit reacts to volume.
questions.where_to_look: Cost-of-sales and expense notes by nature (materials, staff, depreciation, distribution).
hypotheses: H1 Mostly variable: profit stable with volume, exposed to input prices.
H2 Mostly fixed: profit swings with volume.
H3 Mixed.
careful: Staff and distribution are semi-variable.
Depreciation is fixed; materials are variable.
questions.answer_structure: "Variable costs ≈ x% of revenue (mainly [line]); fixed ≈ y% (mainly [line]). Profit is most sensitive to [volume / input prices]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai: depreciation ≈ 11.7% of revenue (fixed-heavy). SADAFCO: materials ≈ 55% (variable-heavy).

questions.question: How much of each riyal goes to materials, and why?
questions.why: Shows where the company starts in the value chain and its commodity exposure.
hypotheses: H1 Integrated: low ratio, cost moved to depreciation and staff.
H2 Converter: high ratio, input includes the supplier's profit.
H3 Ratio moving: commodity cycle or pass-through lag.
careful: A low ratio is not efficiency. Always add the neighbouring lines (depreciation, staff).
questions.answer_structure: "SAR x on materials per SAR 100 of sales vs y for the peer, because [model]. Gross margins end at [a] vs [b]. Risk: [commodity / volume]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 42.0%; SADAFCO 54.9%. Gross margins are equal at ~31%.

questions.question: How productive are its people?
questions.why: Staff costs show automation, scale and labour efficiency.
questions.where_to_look: Staff-cost note; headcount in the annual report.
hypotheses: H1 Productivity rising (automation, scale).
H2 Wage inflation squeezing.
H3 Headcount cut to protect margin.
careful: Integrated firms employ farm staff: compare like with like.
Cuts can be one-offs.
questions.related: Revenue per employee trend; capex in automation.
questions.answer_structure: "Staff costs x% of revenue (from y%); revenue per employee SAR z (±n%). Driver: [reason]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO: staff 19.0% → 14.2% of revenue; headcount 2,783 → 2,501.

questions.question: How much does it spend to sell and distribute, and is it rising?
questions.why: Selling, distribution and marketing show channel cost and brand investment.
questions.where_to_look: Selling & distribution and admin notes; A&P disclosure.
hypotheses: H1 Scale benefit: ratio falling.
H2 Channel power rising: ratio up.
H3 Brand spend cut to protect EBIT.
careful: Cutting A&P raises EBIT now and weakens the brand later.
questions.answer_structure: "SG&A x% of revenue (from y%). A&P z% (from w%). Read: [scale / channel / cut]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO cut A&P from 4.9% to 3.5% in FY25 to protect EBIT. Almarai SG&A 16.7% → 17.2%.

questions.question: What is the gap between EBITDA and EBIT margin, and what does it say?
questions.why: The gap is depreciation: the annual cost of the asset base.
key_ratio: EBITDA margin − EBIT margin = depreciation ÷ revenue
hypotheses: H1 Large gap: asset-heavy model.
H2 Small gap: asset-light.
H3 Gap rising: new plants starting depreciation.
careful: EBITDA ignores the cost of capital. Asset-heavy firms look better on EBITDA than on EBIT.
questions.answer_structure: "EBITDA x%, EBIT y%: depreciation takes z pts, because [assets]. Valuation: compare on EBIT, not EBITDA."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 25.2% vs 13.5% (gap ~11.7 pts). SADAFCO 17.3% vs 13.4% (gap ~3.9 pts).

questions.question: Which cost lines moved the EBIT margin this year?
questions.why: A margin bridge turns a vague change into named causes with sizes.
questions.where_to_look: Common-size income statement, two years side by side.
key_ratio: Change in each line ÷ revenue (pts), summing to the EBIT margin change
hypotheses: H1 One line explains most of it.
H2 Several small moves.
H3 One-offs explain it.
careful: Remove one-offs first.
Check that the bridge adds up to the total.
questions.answer_structure: "EBIT margin fell from x% to y% (−n pts): [line] −a, [line] +b, other ±c. Main cause: [line], [permanent / cyclical]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO FY25: materials −4.6 pts, partly offset by lower staff costs and A&P.

questions.question: How much does profit swing when volume changes?
questions.why: High operating leverage magnifies both good and bad years.
hypotheses: H1 High DOL: fixed-cost heavy, volume is the risk.
H2 Low DOL: variable-cost heavy, prices are the risk.
H3 Reported DOL is meaningless this year.
careful: %ΔEBIT ÷ %Δrevenue only works when prices and costs are stable.
Using this year's DOL to predict this year is circular.
CWIP has no P&L cost: it does not create operating leverage.
questions.answer_structure: "Contribution x%, EBIT y%: DOL ≈ z. A 10% volume fall cuts EBIT by ~10z%. The risk year is [volume fall / input shock]."
questions.worked_example: Exercise split: Almarai DOL ≈ 50 ÷ 13.5 ≈ 3.7; SADAFCO ≈ 37 ÷ 13.4 ≈ 2.8.

questions.question: Does revenue growth reach operating profit?
questions.why: Growth that does not reach NOPAT creates no value.
hypotheses: H1 Profit grows faster: operating leverage.
H2 Profit grows slower: costs rising.
H3 Profit falls: margin shock.
careful: Use normalised EBIT. Net profit can be propped up by finance income or capitalised interest.
questions.answer_structure: "Revenue +x%, NOPAT +y%. The gap of n pts comes from [line]. Growth [creates / does not create] value."
questions.worked_example: 2025: Almarai revenue +5.2%, NOPAT +0.4%. SADAFCO revenue +5.0%, NOPAT −16.6%.

questions.question: What is the normal margin across a full cycle?
questions.why: A DCF needs a normal margin, not the best or worst year.
questions.where_to_look: Five to ten years of margins.
hypotheses: H1 Today is near the average.
H2 Today is a trough: upside.
H3 Today is a peak: downside.
careful: Five years may hold only one commodity cycle.
Structural change can make old averages irrelevant.
questions.answer_structure: "Margin range [low]–[high], average x%. Today y% = [trough / average / peak]. Normal margin for the DCF: z%, because [reason]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO EBIT margin: trough 10.9% (FY22), average 14.1%, FY25 12.3% (normalised). Almarai 12.6%–16.3%.

questions.question: What is not repeatable in this year's profit?
questions.why: Value depends on repeatable profit only.
questions.where_to_look: Other income note; provisions note; gains on disposal; grants.
hypotheses: H1 Clean earnings.
H2 One-off gains inflate profit.
H3 Provision releases inflate profit.
careful: Check the ordinary explanation before the suspicious one.
One-offs can be negative too.
questions.answer_structure: "Reported profit x; one-offs y (list). Normalised profit z = n× reported. The DCF uses z."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO FY25: normalised profit 0.78× reported (property gain, provision releases).

questions.question: Did the margin change because of what was sold (mix) or because each segment's margin changed (rate)?
questions.why: Mix and rate need different actions.
key_ratio: Mix effect = Σ(Δ weight × last year's margin)
Rate effect = Σ(this year's weight × Δ margin)
hypotheses: H1 Rate effect dominates: cost or price problem.
H2 Mix effect dominates: portfolio shift.
H3 Both.
careful: Segment profit definitions must stay the same across years.
questions.answer_structure: "Group margin changed −n pts: rate −a, mix −b. Cause: [segment / line]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO FY25: −4.0 pts, of which −3.9 pts rate (input costs), almost nothing from mix.

questions.question: What tax rate turns EBIT into NOPAT, effective or marginal?
questions.why: The tax rate drives NOPAT and the debt tax shield.
questions.where_to_look: Tax or zakat note; effective rate history.
key_ratio: Effective rate = tax ÷ profit before tax
hypotheses: H1 Effective ≈ marginal.
H2 Effective below marginal (incentives) → converge in the DCF.
H3 Zakat regime: low rate, small tax shield.
careful: Zakat is levied on a base, not on profit: the percentage moves for reasons unrelated to operations.
questions.answer_structure: "Effective rate x%, marginal y%. NOPAT uses [rate] because [reason]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai ~5.4%; SADAFCO ~5%. Debt shield under zakat is small.

questions.question: Which cost line explains the margin gap with the peer?
questions.why: Peer comparison names the source of advantage.
key_ratio: Peer gap by line (pts of revenue)
hypotheses: H1 Gross margin gap: product or input advantage.
H2 SG&A gap: scale or channel.
H3 Depreciation gap: business model.
careful: Different classification of the same cost between companies.
questions.answer_structure: "Margin gap n pts: [line] a, [line] b, [line] c. Source: [advantage]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai vs SADAFCO: materials −13 pts, depreciation +8 pts, gross margin ≈ 0.

questions.question: Is the forecast margin consistent with history and with the cost structure?
questions.why: The forecast margin is often the biggest lever in the valuation.
questions.where_to_look: Budget or DCF inputs vs OP-13.
hypotheses: H1 Forecast within the historical range.
H2 Forecast above the range: must be argued.
H3 Forecast below: conservative.
careful: Do not assume margin recovery: name the cost line that will recover, and by how much.
questions.answer_structure: "Forecast x% vs history [range]. To reach it, [line] must improve n pts because [evidence]. Each pt is worth SAR v a share."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO base 13.0% vs FY25 12.3%; market implies 10.1%; 1 pt ≈ SAR 22 a share.

questions.question: How much capital is tied up in operations, and what is in it?
questions.why: Invested capital is the denominator of ROC: the money that must earn its cost.
questions.where_to_look: Balance sheet; leases; cash and investments note.
key_ratio: Invested capital = debt + equity − cash and investments
hypotheses: H1 Mostly fixed assets.
H2 Mostly working capital.
H3 Large non-operating items (cash, investments, goodwill).
careful: Remove cash and financial investments.
Decide on goodwill and leases consistently.
questions.answer_structure: "Invested capital SAR x: fixed assets a%, working capital b%, CWIP c%."
questions.worked_example: Almarai SAR 33.0bn (of which 5.8bn CWIP). SADAFCO SAR 1.2bn.

questions.question: How much revenue does each riyal of capital produce?
questions.why: Turnover is the second driver of ROC and decides how cheap growth is.
key_ratio: Capital turnover = revenue ÷ average invested capital
hypotheses: H1 High turnover: asset-light model.
H2 Low turnover: asset-heavy model.
H3 Falling turnover: capital added ahead of revenue.
careful: Do not explain turnover with debt: financing does not change it.
Total assets includes cash: avoid it here.
questions.answer_structure: "SAR x of revenue per SAR 100 of capital vs y for the peer. The gap comes from [asset types], see INV-03."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO 2.66× (SAR 257 per 100); Almarai 0.71× (SAR 67 per 100).

questions.question: Which assets explain the turnover gap, and how much each?
questions.why: An additive breakdown sizes each cause.
key_ratio: Capital per SAR 100 of sales = 100 ÷ turnover, split by asset type
hypotheses: H1 Fixed assets explain most.
H2 Working capital explains most.
H3 CWIP (temporary) explains most.
careful: Ratios of ratios cannot be split; use the additive form.
Separate permanent from temporary.
questions.answer_structure: "Per SAR 100 of sales: working capital a vs b, CWIP c vs d, fixed e vs f. Main cause: [line] (n% of the gap), [permanent / temporary]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 150 vs SADAFCO 39: fixed +76, CWIP +23, working capital +12.

questions.question: How capital-intensive is the business, and how old are its assets?
questions.why: Old assets flatter ROC and signal future capex.
questions.where_to_look: Fixed-asset note: gross cost, accumulated depreciation, asset classes.
key_ratio: Asset age ≈ accumulated depreciation ÷ gross PPE
hypotheses: H1 Heavy and new: high capital, low ROC now.
H2 Light: low capital need.
H3 Old assets: high ROC today, replacement coming.
careful: Leased assets sit outside PPE.
Biological assets (herds) follow different rules.
questions.answer_structure: "Net PPE x% of revenue; assets about y% depreciated. Implication: [capex need / ROC quality]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai owns land, herds, farms, plants and fleet; SADAFCO owns plants, freezers and fleet.

questions.question: Is the company maintaining its assets or growing them?
questions.why: Capex above depreciation means growth investment; below means under-investment.
hypotheses: H1 ≈1×: maintenance only.
H2 >1.5×: growth phase.
H3 <1×: under-investment, flattering cash flow.
careful: Depreciation is historical cost; maintenance at today's prices may be higher.
Include new leases and herd capex.
questions.answer_structure: "Capex x× depreciation (history y×). Phase: [maintenance / growth / under-investment]. Cash effect: FCFF [sign]."

questions.question: How much capital is not yet producing, and when will it start?
questions.why: CWIP lowers turnover today and should lift revenue later.
questions.where_to_look: Fixed-asset note (CWIP); capex plan; capitalised interest note.
hypotheses: H1 Plants on schedule: turnover recovers.
H2 Delays: capital sits idle longer.
H3 Over-capacity: turnover never recovers.
careful: CWIP has no P&L cost until it runs: the cost arrives later as depreciation.
Capitalised interest moves a financing cost out of the P&L.
questions.related: ROC on producing capital; coverage incl. capitalised interest (FIN-04).
questions.answer_structure: "CWIP SAR x (y% of capital), due [year]. When it runs it adds SAR z of depreciation and needs SAR w of revenue to earn WACC."
questions.worked_example: Almarai CWIP SAR 5.8bn (18% of invested capital); about a third of interest is capitalised.

questions.question: How much working capital does each riyal of sales need?
questions.why: Every extra riyal of sales ties up this much cash.
questions.where_to_look: Balance sheet: stock, receivables, payables, accruals.
hypotheses: H1 Low: suppliers fund operations.
H2 High: stock or credit heavy.
H3 Rising: worsening terms or growth.
careful: Year-end balances can be unusual (seasonality).
Use trade items only for the day ratios.
questions.answer_structure: "Working capital x% of revenue (history y%). Each SAR 100 of new sales needs SAR x. Driver: [line]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 18.7%; SADAFCO 6.8%.

questions.question: How fast do customers pay?
questions.why: Rising DSO can mean channel stuffing or weaker customers.
hypotheses: H1 Stable: normal.
H2 Rising: looser credit or stuffing.
H3 Falling: tighter collection.
careful: Check the ordinary explanation first (mix of channels, timing).
questions.answer_structure: "DSO x days (history y). Read: [stable / rising / falling], because [reason]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai ~30 days; SADAFCO ~37 days; both stable for six years.

questions.question: How much stock does it hold, and why?
questions.why: Stock protects supply but ties up cash.
questions.where_to_look: Inventory note (raw materials, finished goods, provisions).
key_ratio: DIO = average inventory ÷ cost of sales × 365
hypotheses: H1 Strategic stock of imported inputs.
H2 Slow-moving goods.
H3 Seasonal build-up.
careful: Inventory provisions can move profit.
Split raw materials from finished goods.
questions.answer_structure: "DIO x days: raw materials a, finished goods b. Reason: [strategic / slow / seasonal]. Risk: [provision]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai ~141 days (feed stockpile); SADAFCO ~85 days (powder, packaging).

questions.question: How long does it take to pay suppliers?
questions.why: Payables fund operations; a fall in DPO absorbs cash.
key_ratio: DPO = average trade payables ÷ cost of sales × 365
hypotheses: H1 Strength: suppliers give terms.
H2 Falling: suppliers tightening.
H3 Rising: stretching suppliers (strain).
careful: Rising DPO can be strain, not strength.
questions.answer_structure: "DPO x days (history y). Read: [strength / tightening / strain]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO DPO 47 → 34 days in FY25: watch supplier terms.

questions.question: How long is the cash cycle, and what moves it?
questions.why: The cash cycle summarises how long cash is locked in operations.
key_ratio: Cash conversion cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO
hypotheses: H1 Driven by stock.
H2 Driven by payables.
H3 Driven by customers.
careful: Explain the change by the component that moved.
questions.answer_structure: "Cash cycle x days (from y). The change came from [component] (±n days)."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 132 days (stock). SADAFCO 87 days (from 76), driven by payables.

questions.question: How much of NOPAT is reinvested, and what growth should it buy?
questions.why: Growth must be paid for: reinvestment × ROC gives the growth it can fund.
key_ratio: Reinvestment = net capex + Δ working capital
hypotheses: H1 Fundamental growth ≈ actual: consistent.
H2 Fundamental > actual: capital not yet earning.
H3 Actual > fundamental: margin-led or unsustainable.
careful: Exclude capitalised interest from reinvestment (it is financing).
questions.answer_structure: "Reinvestment rate x% × ROC y% = fundamental growth z% vs actual w%. Gap explained by [reason]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 144% of NOPAT in 2025 (FCFF −1.2bn). SADAFCO 20% × 33.9% = 6.8%.

questions.question: What is the return on capital, and does it come from margin or from turnover?
questions.why: ROC is where operations meet capital. Compared with WACC, it decides value.
key_ratio: ROC = NOPAT ÷ average IC = after-tax margin × turnover
hypotheses: H1 Margin-led.
H2 Turnover-led.
H3 Both.
careful: Use average capital, annualise short periods.
ROC is not ROE: ignore financing here.
questions.answer_structure: "ROC x% = margin a% × turnover b×. The strength is [margin / turnover] because [business reason]."

questions.question: What is the return on capital that is already producing?
questions.why: Removing CWIP separates the business today from the projects of tomorrow.
key_ratio: ROC on producing capital = NOPAT ÷ (IC − CWIP)
hypotheses: H1 Small gap: little idle capital.
H2 Large gap: big projects under way.
H3 Producing ROC also low: the core is weak.
careful: This is a fairness check, not a reason to ignore CWIP.
questions.answer_structure: "ROC on producing capital x% vs y% total: CWIP costs n pts today."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 10.9% vs 9.1%. SADAFCO 36.5% vs 33.9%.

questions.question: What has the new capital actually earned?
questions.why: Value depends on the return on the next riyal, not the average.
questions.where_to_look: NOPAT and capital over several years.
key_ratio: Incremental ROC = Δ NOPAT ÷ Δ invested capital (multi-year, lagged)
hypotheses: H1 New capital earns above WACC: growth creates value.
H2 Earns about WACC: growth adds nothing.
H3 Earns below WACC: growth destroys value.
careful: Year-by-year ratios explode when capital barely moves.
Margin recovery on old capital looks like a return on new capital.
questions.answer_structure: "Over [window] NOPAT rose x on y of new capital: z%. Corrected for [margin recovery], about w%."
questions.worked_example: Almarai ~17% (flattered); poultry ~7.6%. SADAFCO ~96% (margin recovery); non-drinks ~0% FY20–23.

questions.question: Which segment earns its capital, and where does new capital go?
questions.why: Capital flowing to the weakest segment lowers group ROC.
key_ratio: Share of new assets by segment
hypotheses: H1 New capital goes to the best segment.
H2 To the weakest segment.
H3 Spread evenly.
careful: Segment profit is usually after allocations and before tax: rank, do not compare with WACC directly.
questions.answer_structure: "[Segment] absorbed x% of new assets and earns y%. [Segment] earns z% on few assets."
questions.worked_example: Almarai poultry absorbed all net new segment capital (SAR 3.6bn), earning 7.6%.

questions.question: What did acquisitions cost, and what do they earn?
questions.why: Acquisitions are investments: the price paid sets the return.
key_ratio: Return on acquisition = acquired NOPAT ÷ price paid
hypotheses: H1 Paid fairly, returns above WACC.
H2 Overpaid: goodwill large, returns low.
H3 Too small to matter.
careful: ROC excluding goodwill flatters management's record.
questions.answer_structure: "Paid SAR x for [target]; it earns y% on the price. Verdict: [creates / destroys] value."
questions.worked_example: Almarai's 2022 bakery acquisition sits inside its +18% growth year.

questions.question: Do its investments earn more than they cost?
questions.why: Value is created only when ROC exceeds WACC; growth multiplies the spread.
hypotheses: H1 Large positive spread: growth creates value.
H2 Thin spread: growth adds little.
H3 Negative: growth destroys value.
careful: Use the WACC of each year when judging history.
questions.answer_structure: "ROC x% vs WACC y%: spread n pts, EVA SAR v m. Growth [creates / adds little / destroys] value."
questions.worked_example: Almarai spread +1.7 pts (EVA SAR 513m). SADAFCO +26.6 pts (EVA ~SAR 300m).

questions.question: How is the capital financed: debt versus equity, at market value?
questions.why: The mix sets risk and WACC. It is a financing decision, separate from investment.
key_ratio: Debt weight = debt ÷ (debt + market value of equity)
hypotheses: H1 Mostly equity: low risk, maybe idle capacity to borrow.
H2 Moderate debt.
H3 High debt: risk rises with the cycle.
careful: Use market values for WACC, book values for covenants.
questions.answer_structure: "Debt is x% of capital at market value (book y%). Read: [conservative / moderate / aggressive]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 23.3%; SADAFCO 0.9% (leases only).

questions.question: What counts as debt beyond bank loans?
questions.why: Leases, end-of-service benefits and put options are debt-like claims on the firm.
questions.where_to_look: Leases note; employee benefits note; NCI put options.
key_ratio: Total debt = borrowings + leases (+ debt-like items in the equity bridge)
hypotheses: H1 Bank debt only.
H2 Leases material.
H3 Large debt-like items (pensions, puts).
careful: Treat each item the same way in ROC, WACC and the equity bridge.
questions.answer_structure: "Debt SAR x = borrowings a + leases b; debt-like items c deducted in the bridge."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO: no bank debt; leases 70m, EOSB 171m. Almarai: borrowings 12.5bn + leases 0.55bn.

questions.question: How many years of operating cash would repay the debt?
questions.why: Net debt ÷ EBITDA is the lenders' first test.
hypotheses: H1 <1×: conservative.
H2 1–3×: normal for stable food.
H3 >3×: stretched.
careful: Rising leverage during a capex peak may be planned: check the path.
questions.answer_structure: "Net debt x× EBITDA (from y×), driven by [capex / payout]. Path: [peak year, then …]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 2.25× (peak in 2026 in the budget). SADAFCO net cash 573m (−1.1×).

questions.question: How easily does operating profit cover interest?
questions.why: Coverage sets the rating and the cost of debt.
key_ratio: Economic coverage = EBIT ÷ gross interest (incl. capitalised)
hypotheses: H1 High coverage: safe.
H2 Falling coverage: debt growing faster than EBIT.
H3 Reported coverage flattered by capitalised interest.
careful: Capitalised interest hides part of the cost from the P&L.
questions.answer_structure: "Economic coverage x× (reported y×). The gap is capitalised interest. Rating implied: [rating]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 4.1× economic vs 6.6× reported. SADAFCO 116× (lease interest only).

questions.question: What happens to coverage in a bad year?
questions.why: A partner checks the rating in the downside, not only today.
hypotheses: H1 Safe even in stress.
H2 Rating drops one notch.
H3 Covenant risk.
careful: Use the stress that matches the business (feed shock, volume fall).
questions.answer_structure: "With EBIT −30%, coverage falls to x×, which implies [rating]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 2.9× (just below the 3.0× BBB line). SADAFCO 81×.

questions.question: What does the company pay to borrow, and why?
questions.why: The cost of debt follows the rating and the country risk.
key_ratio: Pre-tax cost of debt = risk-free + country spread + company spread
hypotheses: H1 Synthetic rating matches actual borrowing cost.
H2 Actual is lower (relationship banks, subsidy).
H3 Actual is higher (risk).
careful: Use the right size table (small vs large firm).
questions.answer_structure: "Synthetic rating [x] → cost of debt y% pre-tax, z% after tax."
questions.worked_example: Almarai A3/A− (~5.6%). SADAFCO AAA (5.1%) on the small-firm table.

questions.question: When is the debt due, and can it be refinanced?
questions.why: Short maturities in a bad year are how solid companies fail.
hypotheses: H1 Long-dated, facilities available.
H2 Concentrated maturities.
H3 Reliance on short-term funding.
careful: Undrawn facilities can be withdrawn in a crisis.
questions.answer_structure: "x% of debt due within a year; undrawn facilities SAR y. Refinancing risk: [low / moderate / high]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 12.6% short-term, SAR 7.5bn undrawn: moderate.

questions.question: Can it get through the next 12 months?
questions.why: Liquidity is about the short term; solvency about the long term.
key_ratio: Months of cash costs covered by cash
hypotheses: H1 Comfortable.
H2 Tight but funded by facilities.
H3 Stretched.
careful: A falling cash pile can be a payout choice, not a problem.
questions.answer_structure: "Current x×, quick y×, cash covers z months of costs. Trend: [direction], because [reason]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO current 2.1×, quick 1.3×, 3.1 months of costs (from 5.7).

questions.question: Does profit turn into cash?
questions.why: Profit that does not become cash cannot pay dividends or debt.
key_ratio: Accrual ratio = (net profit − CFO) ÷ average assets
hypotheses: H1 CFO ≥ profit: good quality.
H2 CFO < profit: working capital build or non-cash gains.
H3 Persistently low: quality concern.
careful: Asset-heavy firms show high CFO because of depreciation: test free cash flow.
Check ordinary causes first.
questions.answer_structure: "CFO x× profit (average y×). Gap due to [reason]. Quality: [good / watch]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai CFO ≈ 2× profit (depreciation). SADAFCO 0.94× in FY25 (non-cash reversals).

questions.question: How much cash is left after reinvestment, and for whom?
questions.why: FCFF is what the DCF values; FCFE is what shareholders can receive.
key_ratio: FCFE = CFO + interest effects − capex − lease and debt repayments
hypotheses: H1 Positive and stable.
H2 Negative due to a growth phase.
H3 Negative due to weak operations.
careful: Negative FCFF in a capex phase can be fine if returns follow.
questions.answer_structure: "FCFF SAR x (NOPAT a − reinvestment b). Read: [mature / investing / weak]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai FCFF −1.2bn (2025). SADAFCO FCFF +305m.

questions.question: Is the dividend funded by free cash or by borrowing?
questions.why: A dividend above free cash is paid from debt or from the cash pile.
hypotheses: H1 Covered by free cash.
H2 Above free cash: borrowed or from savings.
H3 Special dividend, one-off.
careful: Payout above 100% can be a deliberate return of excess cash.
questions.answer_structure: "Payout x% of profit and y× FCFE. Funded by [free cash / debt / cash pile]. Sustainable at [level]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO 114% of profit, 1.7× FCFE. Almarai 40% of profit but FCFE negative: partly borrowed.

questions.question: How fast can it grow without new capital?
questions.why: Sustainable growth links payout, ROE and growth.
key_ratio: Sustainable growth = ROE × b ÷ (1 − ROE × b), b = 1 − payout
hypotheses: H1 Sustainable ≥ actual: self-funded.
H2 Sustainable < actual: needs debt or equity.
H3 Negative: equity shrinking.
careful: High-ROC firms can grow on little reinvestment even when retention is low.
questions.answer_structure: "Sustainable growth x% vs actual y%. Gap funded by [debt / cash / high ROC]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO −3.6% at a 114% payout; growth relies on 30%+ ROC on small reinvestment.

questions.question: Is ROE driven by the business or by financing?
questions.why: ROE above ROC comes from debt; below ROC comes from idle cash.
key_ratio: ROE ≈ ROC + (ROC − after-tax cost of debt) × D/E
Share of ROE from leverage = (ROE − ROC) ÷ ROE
hypotheses: H1 ROE > ROC: leverage lifts returns, and risk.
H2 ROE < ROC: cash drag.
H3 ROE ≈ ROC.
careful: Higher ROE from debt is not value creation by itself.
questions.answer_structure: "ROE x% vs ROC y%: [leverage adds / cash subtracts] n pts. The business itself earns y%."
questions.worked_example: Almarai ROE 12.5% > ROC 9.1% (debt). SADAFCO 26.9% < 33.9% (cash drag).

questions.question: What return do shareholders require?
questions.why: Cost of equity is most of WACC for low-debt firms.
questions.where_to_look: Damodaran betas, ERP, country risk; market data.
key_ratio: Cost of equity = risk-free + levered beta × ERP
hypotheses: H1 Industry beta fits the business.
H2 Geography raises the ERP.
H3 Company-specific risk not captured.
careful: Mixing ERP methods (rating vs CDS).
Regression betas of one stock are noisy: prefer bottom-up.
questions.related: ERP sensitivity; reverse DCF implied ERP.
questions.answer_structure: "Cost of equity x% = rf a% + β b × ERP c%. Judgement calls: [beta / ERP]."
questions.worked_example: Both: βu 0.61, rf 4.18%, Saudi ERP 5.01%. Almarai revenue-weighted ERP would be 6.17%.

questions.question: What is the overall cost of capital, and would more debt lower it?
questions.why: WACC is the hurdle for ROC and the discount rate in the DCF.
questions.where_to_look: Cost of equity; after-tax cost of debt; market weights.
key_ratio: WACC = E/V × ke + D/V × kd × (1 − t)
hypotheses: H1 Optimal structure.
H2 Under-levered: debt could lower WACC.
H3 Over-levered: risk raises WACC.
careful: Under zakat the debt tax shield is small: more debt barely lowers WACC.
questions.answer_structure: "WACC x% (ke a%, kd after tax b%, debt weight c%). More debt would [lower / not lower] it because [tax regime]."
questions.worked_example: Almarai 7.46%; SADAFCO 7.24%.

questions.question: Is debt in the same currency as revenue, and are rates fixed or floating?
questions.why: Mismatches turn currency moves or rate rises into losses.
questions.where_to_look: Debt note (currency, rate type); FX note.
hypotheses: H1 Matched currencies, fixed rates.
H2 Floating rates: exposed to SAIBOR.
H3 Foreign-currency debt against local revenue.
careful: Pegged currencies (SAR/USD) reduce but do not remove risk in subsidiaries.
questions.answer_structure: "x% floating; y% in foreign currency. A 1 pt rate rise costs SAR z m."
questions.worked_example: Almarai has Egyptian and Jordanian operations; SAR is pegged to USD.

questions.question: Is surplus cash a strength or idle capital?
questions.why: Cash earning less than the cost of equity dilutes returns.
key_ratio: Yield on cash vs cost of equity
hypotheses: H1 Strategic buffer.
H2 Idle capital: return it or invest it.
H3 Being paid out already.
careful: Value cash separately in the DCF, never inside FCFF.
questions.answer_structure: "Cash SAR x (y% of assets) earns z% vs ke w%. Use: [buffer / return / invest]."
questions.worked_example: SADAFCO cash and investments 1,062m → 644m; 24% of assets earning ~5%.

questions.question: Does this decision change value, or only ROE and risk?
questions.why: Investment decisions create value; financing decisions mostly move risk and ROE.
questions.where_to_look: Any proposal: buyback, borrowing, capex, acquisition.
key_ratio: vs Δ tax shield − Δ distress cost (financing)
hypotheses: H1 Investment decision: judge by ROC vs WACC.
H2 Financing decision: judge by tax shield vs risk.
H3 Mixed: separate the two parts.
careful: "ROE goes up, so it is good" is the classic trap.
questions.answer_structure: "This is a [investment / financing] decision. Value changes only through [channel], worth about SAR x. ROE rises, but [risk effect]."
questions.worked_example: "Borrow SAR 1bn to buy back SADAFCO shares": a financing decision; under zakat the tax shield is small, so value barely changes while risk rises.
